subsection: 8. The co-operative movement and industrial Belfast: the shipyards

notes.h: Why Irish farmers needed help: the problems behind co-operation
notes.b: By the 1880s most Irish farmers worked small tenant holdings and were squeezed by prices, debt and foreign competition. The co-operative movement was an attempt to solve these problems by self-help while the land question was moving towards tenant ownership.
points: Most farms were small and rented from landlords. The agricultural depression of 1877-79 hit tenants hard, and land reform was by then moving towards tenant ownership of the land.
Irish farmers sold their produce badly. Each made butter in a small way at home, so quality varied and prices were poor, because buyers could not rely on the product.
New competition came from imports, above all Danish butter, which was better made and graded, so it fetched higher prices than Irish butter.
Denmark had answered the same pressure by organising farmer-owned co-operative creameries (dairies that process milk into butter), and this became the model Irish reformers copied.
Many farmers depended on gombeen men, the local shopkeepers and moneylenders who sold goods and lent money on credit at high prices and high interest. This kept small farmers permanently in debt.
notes.tip: For a question on who and why, name the causes: poor marketing, dependence on gombeen men and competition from Danish butter, plus the Danish co-operative model.

notes.h: Horace Plunkett and the origins of the co-operative movement
notes.b: The movement was driven by one man, an unusual figure who was a landowner and a Unionist but wanted to reform Irish farming from below. His background explains both his ideas and the suspicion he met.
points: Horace Plunkett (1854-1932), the son of Lord Dunsany (an Anglo-Irish peer), was an Anglo-Irish landowner. He ranched in Wyoming in the 1880s and returned to Ireland convinced that farmers needed better organisation.

He was a Unionist MP for South Dublin from 1892 to 1900 (he lost the seat in 1900), though he worked with nationalists in his reform schemes, because he believed economic improvement mattered more than the quarrel over Home Rule.

Plunkett took the Danish model of farmer-owned co-operative creameries, where farmers pooled their milk and shared the profits. A creamery used a mechanical cream separator (a machine that separates cream from milk), giving higher quality at lower cost.
The first co-operative creamery is usually dated to 1889 at Dromcollogher, Co. Limerick. The model then spread in Munster and elsewhere.
Plunkett's supporters included Fr Tom Finlay, a Jesuit, and the poet and writer George Russell, who used the pen name AE.
The Irish Homestead, begun in 1895, was the movement's weekly paper, which spread its ideas to farmers. AE edited it from 1905, so here he matters as a co-operator and editor.
notes.tip: Do not mix up Plunkett (Unionist, co-operation) with Davitt or Parnell (land) or Larkin (labour). Say the first creamery is 'usually dated' to 1889 at Dromcollogher.

notes.h: The IAOS, credit societies and the growth of co-operation
notes.b: One creamery was not a movement. In 1894 Plunkett founded a central body to promote, advise and check co-operative societies across the country, and the idea spread beyond dairying.
points: The Irish Agricultural Organisation Society (IAOS) was founded in 1894 by Plunkett to organise, advise and inspect co-operative societies.
Its motto was "better farming, better business, better living", a short statement of its self-help philosophy: farmers improving their own lives without waiting for the state.

Co-operative creameries multiplied in the 1890s, giving small dairy farmers a market and a share of the profits. They introduced mechanical cream separators and bought milk by its fat content, which rewarded quality and raised the standard of Irish butter.
Credit societies were modelled on German Raiffeisen banks. They lent small sums to members on the guarantee of their neighbours, which reduced dependence on gombeen men.
Other societies supplied seeds and fertiliser and sold eggs and poultry. The Irish Agricultural Wholesale Society (IAWS), the movement's wholesale body, was founded in 1897.
By 1914 there were about 1,000 societies with about 100,000 members (approximate; estimates vary). They were strongest in Munster and weakest in Ulster.
notes.tip: Keep the dates and bodies apart: IAOS 1894 (the organising society), IAWS 1897 (the wholesale society), the Department of Agriculture 1899 (the state department) and the Congested Districts Board 1891. Use 'about' for the society and member numbers.

notes.h: The Recess Committee and the Department of Agriculture (1895-1899)
notes.b: Plunkett believed the state had to back self-help. In 1895 he brought nationalists and unionists together to argue for a government department for farming and industry, and in 1899 he got one.
points: The Recess Committee met during the parliamentary recess of 1895 (the break when Parliament was not sitting), with Plunkett as chairman. It brought together nationalists and unionists, including Thomas Sinclair, a Belfast Presbyterian unionist, and John Redmond, a nationalist.
Its report in 1896 studied the methods of Denmark, France and Germany and recommended a government department for agriculture and technical education.

The Department of Agriculture and Technical Instruction (DATI) was established in 1899. Plunkett was its vice-president (the effective head) from 1899 to 1907, and the Chief Secretary for Ireland was its president.
DATI's work included agricultural education and instructors, research, technical schools and fisheries, so the state now supported the practical improvement the co-operatives promoted.
Plunkett lost the vice-presidency in 1907 after hostility from the Irish Party, and T.W. Russell succeeded him.
notes.tip: The Recess Committee met in 1895 and reported in 1896, but the Department was only founded in 1899. For an Ordinary Level paragraph on Plunkett, link IAOS 1894, the Danish model, creameries, the Recess Committee, DATI 1899 and his post.

notes.h: Suspicion and results of the movement
notes.b: Co-operation brought clear economic gains, but because Plunkett was a Unionist working across the political divide, many groups distrusted him. Understanding who suspected him, and why, is as important as knowing what the movement achieved.
points: Many nationalists suspected Plunkett, a unionist, of trying to turn farmers away from the land and national questions. Irish Party hostility later cost him his post in 1907, while others, like AE, saw the movement as national self-help.
Many unionists, especially Ulster farmers, were slow to join, partly through suspicion of Plunkett's dealings with nationalists. This is one reason the movement was weakest in Ulster.
The Catholic clergy had often supported local creameries. Even so, a clerical and nationalist campaign contributed to Plunkett's defeat in 1900.
Four years later, Plunkett's book Ireland in the New Century (1904) criticised Catholic influence on Irish initiative, which angered the Church and caused him further problems.
Private creamery owners and shopkeepers resented the competition from co-operatives, because the societies took away their trade.
Results: the co-operatives improved the quality of Irish butter, raised farm incomes, spread the idea of self-help and trained a generation of local leaders.
The movement did not solve the problems of poor western farmers, who were helped more by the Congested Districts Board (founded in 1891).
notes.tip: Expect unionist and nationalist reasons for suspicion, plus the clergy; do not omit the Church. Keep the dates in order: the defeat came in 1900 and the book in 1904.

notes.h: Belfast's growth: from a small town to the largest city in Ireland
notes.b: Most of Ireland stayed farming country, but north-east Ulster shared in the Industrial Revolution. Belfast grew from a small town into Ireland's industrial capital, tied by trade to Britain and the empire.
points: The Industrial Revolution (the shift to factory and machine production) reached north-east Ulster, in linen and shipbuilding, far more than the rest of Ireland. Belfast's trade was tied to Britain and the empire, which supplied its markets and raw materials.
Belfast's population was only about 20,000 around 1800, so the later growth was very rapid. It was given city status in 1888.
The census figures were about 255,000 in 1891 (255,896), about 349,000 in 1901 (349,180) and about 387,000 in 1911 (386,947). In 1891 Belfast passed Dublin city to become the largest city in Ireland.
Catholic workers from the countryside moved into west Belfast, around the Falls Road, because the growing industries offered jobs. By 1911 about a quarter of the city was Catholic.
notes.tip: If asked why Belfast grew, give linen, shipbuilding, the ropeworks and migration, and use the 1891 overtaking of Dublin as the key date. Belfast passed Dublin in 1891, not 1901, and became a city in 1888.

notes.b: Belfast's growth rested on several industries, with linen first and shipbuilding later. Most of them sold to Britain and the empire, which is why the city's prosperity depended on that link.
points: Linen, spun and woven in mills, was the first great industry. Belfast was nicknamed Linenopolis and its mills employed tens of thousands of workers, mostly women and girls.

The American Civil War (1861-65) cut cotton supplies and boosted linen, because buyers turned to the alternative cloth. Power-loom mills (machine weaving) then replaced handloom weaving in people's homes.
The Belfast Ropeworks at Connswater, founded in 1873, was among the largest ropeworks in the world. It supplied rope to shipping across the world.
Tobacco manufacture grew with Gallaher and other firms. Engineering firms such as the Sirocco Works made machinery for export.
Whiskey distilling (Dunville) was another trade, so the city's industry was varied and not tied to one product.

notes.h: Harland and Wolff and Workman Clark: the founding of the shipyards
notes.b: Shipbuilding on Queen's Island made Belfast famous. It began with a small yard, two engineers and a young apprentice who became its driving force.
points: Edward Harland, an English engineer, bought a small yard on Queen's Island in 1858. In 1861 he went into partnership with Gustav Wolff, a German-born engineer from Hamburg, creating Harland and Wolff.
William Pirrie was born in Quebec in 1847 to Ulster parents and joined the yard as an apprentice. He became a partner in 1874 and chairman after Harland's death in 1895.
Pirrie's success was rewarded when he was made Lord Pirrie in 1906, for example. Remember that Harland, not Pirrie, founded the yard; Pirrie led it from 1895.
Workman Clark, founded in 1880 by Frank Workman and George Clark, was the second Belfast yard. It built cargo and passenger ships, so it competed with Harland and Wolff for the shipping trade.
notes.tip: A strong Ordinary Level paragraph on Harland and Wolff gives Harland's purchase (1858), Wolff (1861) and Pirrie (partner 1874, chairman 1895). Do not confuse Edward Harland (English) with Gustav Wolff (German-born), or Harland and Wolff (1858 and 1861) with Workman Clark (1880).

notes.h: The Olympic-class liners, the Titanic and the scale of the yards
notes.b: Harland and Wolff won its fame by building giant liners for the White Star Line. The yards also became the city's biggest employers, so Belfast's prosperity rode on the empire's shipping trade.
points: The firm built ships for the White Star Line, including the Olympic-class liners Olympic (launched 1910), Titanic and Britannic (launched 1914). They were the biggest ships in the world when built.
The Arrol Gantry, built over the slipways in 1908-09 by Sir William Arrol, allowed Olympic and Titanic to be built side by side.
Titanic was launched on 31 May 1911 and sank on her maiden voyage on 15 April 1912 after hitting an iceberg, with the loss of about 1,500 lives.
Harland and Wolff alone employed about 15,000 men by 1912 (approximate). The two yards together employed tens of thousands.
notes.tip: Keep the liners' dates straight: Titanic was launched in 1911 and lost in 1912, and Britannic was launched in 1914. The sinking was a disaster at sea, so do not blame the Belfast shipbuilders for it.

notes.b: Industrial Belfast offered work, but conditions were hard, and jobs were divided by religion. This divide helped link the city's industry to unionism.
points: Mill workers, mostly women and girls, worked long hours in hot, damp rooms full of flax dust (fine fibres from the flax plant), which caused lung disease. Wages were low.
Half-timers (child workers who split their time between school and mill) also worked in the mills. Many mill women were the main earners in their families.
Shipyard work was dangerous, and casual labourers were laid off between contracts, so their income was uncertain.

Skilled jobs in the shipyards and engineering were mainly held by Protestants, helped by family and Orange Order connections (the Orange Order being a Protestant society). Catholics tended to be labourers.
Sectarian riots occurred in Belfast in 1857, 1864 and 1886. The riots of 1886, during the Home Rule crisis of that year, included attacks on Catholic workers at the shipyards.
notes.tip: For working conditions and sectarianism, give mill dust and wages, casual yard labour, Protestant skilled jobs and the 1886 and 1912 events, and name the link to Home Rule. Do not mix up the 1886 riots with the 1912 expulsions.

notes.h: The 1912 expulsions, Larkin's strike and the link to unionism
notes.b: Religious divisions at work exploded in 1912, while an earlier moment of unity had faded. Together with economic self-interest, these events tied Belfast's workers and employers to unionism.
points: In 1907 Larkin's Belfast dockers' strike briefly united Catholic and Protestant workers, but the unity did not last.

In July 1912, during the Home Rule crisis, Protestant workers drove Catholic workers and some Protestant labour sympathisers out of Workman Clark and Harland and Wolff. The numbers were thousands, about 2,000-3,000 by common estimates (estimates vary).
Belfast's Protestant majority opposed Home Rule (a separate Irish parliament). Many Protestant workers feared that Home Rule would bring tariffs (taxes on trade) and Catholic dominance.
Belfast's industries depended on markets in Britain and the empire, so this fear linked industrial interests to unionism.
notes.tip: Name the link to Home Rule: fear of tariffs and Catholic dominance, and economic dependence on Britain and the empire. If you give the number expelled in 1912, write 'thousands' or 'about 2,000-3,000, estimates vary'.

notes.b: The two largest cities in Ireland had different economies, and these shaped their politics. A good comparison links economy to attitudes towards Home Rule.
points: Belfast depended on export manufacturing, mainly linen and shipbuilding, linked to British and imperial markets. Dublin depended on administration, trade, brewing and distilling.
Dublin had large employers such as Guinness at St James's Gate and Jacob's biscuits, but many of its workers were casual and poorly paid.

Skilled shipyard and engineering men in Belfast earned more than Dublin's casual labourers. Belfast's workers lived in terraced streets rather than Dublin-style tenements, though poverty and disease still afflicted the mill districts.
Belfast was strongly Protestant and unionist. Dublin was nationalist, with a strong labour movement.
Belfast's industrial development depended on its link with Britain, which was a major reason for unionist opposition to Home Rule.
Belfast's Catholic minority and Protestant majority lived in separate districts, such as the Catholic Falls and the Protestant Shankill, so the city's politics were territorial as well as economic.
notes.tip: Compare economic base (export manufacturing against administration, trade and brewing), employment (skilled yard work against casual labour) and politics (unionist against nationalist and labour). Strong answers link the economy to opposition to Home Rule.

notes.b: Both developments brought prosperity to part of Ireland, but each left problems unsolved. Examiners reward a clear judgement with named facts on both sides.
points: Achievement: the co-operatives raised the quality of butter and farmers' incomes, and encouraged self-help. Belfast became an industrial city of international importance.
Limit: the co-operatives hardly reached the poor west or Ulster, and drew political suspicion. Belfast's prosperity rested on cheap female labour, harsh conditions and sectarian divisions.
Contemporary nationalists were suspicious of Plunkett as a unionist, while unionists pointed to Belfast as proof of the benefits of the Union.
Historians judge the co-operative movement a success of self-help, though it is often judged less decisive than land reform in modernising Irish farming.
notes.tip: In a paired essay on Belfast industry and the co-operative movement, state what each achieved with dates and named facts, what each did not achieve, and then compare them. A one-sided narrative scores poorly.
